newsitem.title: USA: Tough guy film actor Robert Mitchum dies at 79.
newsitem.headline: Tough guy film actor Robert Mitchum dies at 79.

text.p: Actor Robert Mitchum, the sleepy-eyed, barrel-chested star of more than 125 films that spanned six decades, died early on Tuesday. He was 79.

Mitchum, who starred in the epic TV miniseries "The Winds of War" and "War and Remembrance", died in his sleep at his home in Santa Barbara around 5 a.m. PDT (1200 GMT), according to his agent, Jack Gilardi.
Mitchum had been suffering from emphysema for more than a year and was diagnosed with lung cancer last spring.
"We've not only lost a great man and a great actor but we've also lost a great friend," Gilardi said.
Mitchum had a distinctive baritone voice that allowed him to be vaguely threatening in heroic roles and oddly sympathetic as a villain.
"I was unclassifiable," he said once. "I am not a leading man. I am not a heavy. I enjoy playing heavies, and I can be a most convincing heavy, but really, I just have a baritone voice. That's all."
He also had a rugged, belligerent profile that led to such nicknames as "The Great Stone Face." Mitchum himself said: "I agree with the guy who wrote that I looked like a shark with a broken nose."
He had an image in Hollywood as a "bad boy", which was fuelled by a 1948 arrest for marijuana possession, which led to six months in a work camp.

His workmanlike approach to his craft grew from an unstable past. Born on Aug. 6, 1917, in Bridgeport, Connecticut, he was soon left fatherless and led a gypsy-like childhood, frequently moving, always struggling.
As a young man in the 1930s, he wandered the country and the world, working as an engine wiper on a freighter, a nightclub bouncer, a boxer, a ditchdigger and a publicist for an astrologer.
In 1940 he married his high school sweetheart, Dorothy Spence, and settled down to raising a family and working for a California aircraft company.

Unhappy there, he signed on as an extra in "pictures," as he always called movies. Appearances in Westerns led to bit parts in a string of "B" movies and two big war films, "Cry Havoc" and "Gung Ho!," both released in 1943, a year in which he appeared in 18 films.

In 1944 he won praise for a thriller, "When Strangers Marry," with Kim Novak, and another war film, "Thirty Seconds Over Tokyo," whose director Mervyn LeRoy told him: "You're either the lousiest actor in the world or the best."

In 1945 Mitchum made the big time as the rugged but weary captain of "The Story of GI Joe," based on the war memoirs of war correspondent Ernie Pyle. The role earned Mitchum an Academy Award nomination for best supporting actor, but he did not show up at the ceremony.
Soon he was drafted into the Army and served as a private.
In his early years, especially, he was quick to join some critics in dismissing his acting talent.
"Listen," he said, "I got three expressions: looking left, looking right and looking straight ahead."

But colleagues saw a different man. Charles Laughton, apologising for undercutting Mitchum's tough guy image, branded him "a tender man and a gentleman," while Deborah Kerr called him "a poet who won't show his poetry."

"I figure I'm doing a job," Mitchum later offered. "That I understand. Like a plumber. I'm a good plumber. I show up on time, bring my tools so I don't have to make two trips, say the jokes, punch out and go home."

During the 1940s and 1950s he appeared in several "films noirs", including "Out of the Past" (1947), a private-eye thriller with Jane Greer. But the following year he played directly against that type, singing opposite Loretta Young in "Rachel and the Stranger".
That same year he also starred in one of his best Westerns, playing a heroic stranger in "Blood on the Moon."

His marijuana arrest that year threatened his career, but he treated it with typical tough guy aplomb. Asked what the work camp was like, he replied: "Just like Palm Springs. Without the riff-raff, of course."

In 1949 he appeared in "The Red Pony," but a string of forgettable movies followed. In 1954 Mitchum played Marilyn Monroe's laconic escort in the hit "River of No Return" and also scored big as a selfish doctor in "Not As a Stranger."

Another of his best roles, and one of his most complex, came a year later with "The Night of the Hunter," an acclaimed but less financially successful film in which he played a murderous preacher with the words "love" and "hate" tattooed on his knuckles.
Hits and misses followed through the 1960s. Successes included "Heaven Knows, Mr. Allison" (1957), "Home From the Hill" (1960), "The Sundowners" (1960), "Cape Fear" (1962) and "El Dorado" (1967).

In the 1970s, Mitchum turned aside thoughts of retiring and starred as a remorseful wife-murderer in "Going Home" (1971), a defrocked priest in "The Wrath of God" (1972) and a tired crook in "The Friends of Eddie Coyle" (1975).
In 1975 he was brilliantly cast as the laconic detective Philip Marlowe in a remake of Raymond Chandler's "Farewell My Lovely," a role he repeated in 1978 in "The Big Sleep."

In 1980 Mitchum reversed his stand against television and agreed to do a TV movie, the 16-hour miniseries "The Winds of War." As Navy Capt. Pug Henry, his stern but human presence gave a solid centre to a show otherwise steeped in soap opera.
In 1991 he appeared in Martin Scorsese's remake of "Cape Fear", with Robert De Niro and Nick Nolte.

Despite brief separations in 1948 and 1953, Mitchum remained married to his wife Dorothy. Of their three children, his sons James and Christopher have occasionally acted and his daughter Petrine, worked for a movie production company.
